"I keep hearing it, Aparna-didi. Nani said, 'Come when your exams finish, no hurry.' And I said, 'Next month, promise.'"
Aparna set down the steel tumblers. "Rukmini, that's the fourth time this week you've told me about that call."
"Because if I'd taken the Friday bus instead of waiting for results, I'd have seen her. I'd have noticed she was breathless. I'd have—"
"You'd have what? Stopped her heart from doing what it did?"
Rukmini twisted her dupatta around her fingers. "At least then it would properly be my fault. Now it's just... nothing I can hold."
Aparna sat beside her on the divan. "Amma says the same about not calling the doctor that Sunday. Three months, and you two keep taking turns blaming yourselves."
"So what do I do with it?"
"Say it to me instead of to the ceiling at two in the morning. And maybe you try the counselling centre at your college. I'll come with you the first time."

qa.a: Rukmini said, 'Next month, promise,' after Nani told her to come when her exams finished.

qa.q: Why might Rukmini wish the death were 'properly' her fault?
qa.a: Blaming herself gives her something to hold on to; guilt feels easier than accepting that Nani's death was never in her hands.

qa.q: What turning point is open to Rukmini at this stage?
qa.a: She can say the what-ifs out loud to Aparna instead of looping alone at night, and take up the offer to visit the college counselling centre together.

qa.q: How is Aparna affected as she listens to her sister?
qa.a: Aparna is grieving Nani too, and she is watching both Amma and Rukmini blame themselves, so she is trying to steady the family while carrying her own loss.

grounding: Shows a young adult replaying the last phone call and clinging to self-blame as a false sense of control months after a death.

My name is Kamal, and for most of last winter I lived inside a four-minute phone call. Dadu rang on a Tuesday to ask whether the Pune rains had stopped. I was late for a birthday dinner, so I said, "I'll call you Sunday, I'm coming home in December anyway." He died on Thursday.
For months I rebuilt that call. If I had stayed on longer. If I had booked the October train. If I had heard something in his cough. Every version ended with me catching it in time and getting him to a hospital.
Looking back, those what-ifs were oddly comforting, like I still had my hands on a steering wheel. Rukmini, my lab partner, finally asked me one evening, "Would the doctors in Guwahati have done anything different because you were in the room?" I didn't have an answer. That was the first night in weeks I slept straight through.

qa.q: How long was Kamal's last phone call with Dadu?
qa.a: It was a four-minute phone call.

qa.q: Why did the what-ifs feel 'oddly comforting' to Kamal?
qa.a: Every imagined version ended with Kamal catching the illness in time, so the guilt gave a feeling of still having hands on a steering wheel.

qa.q: What helped Kamal step out of the loop, and what else could help if it came back?
qa.a: Rukmini's plain question about whether being in the room would have changed anything loosened it; if the loop returns, talking it through with a friend or a college counsellor could help.

qa.q: How might Rukmini have felt before asking that question?
qa.a: Rukmini may have been unsure how to help a grieving lab partner, and chose a calm, factual question rather than simply saying 'don't blame yourself'.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult looping on what-ifs about a last call and how that guilt felt like control over a death that was out of reach.

Mahima, sit. You asked why your Deepak Mama went quiet at the sweet shop just now. Let me tell you.
When I was nineteen, my Amma died in the April of my second year. By October I thought I was fine. Marks were back up, I was laughing in the canteen again. Then one morning in the chemistry lecture, someone behind me opened a tiffin of besan laddoos. Amma's Diwali smell, cardamom and roasted gram flour. My eyes just flooded. I had to walk out with the whole class staring.
I sat on the stairs thinking, six months of progress, gone. I was so ashamed.
It took me years to understand I hadn't slipped back at all. Grief moves like the tide, beta. It goes out, it comes in, and the coming in doesn't cancel the going out. Today at the shop was just another wave.

qa.a: Besan laddoos from a tiffin behind him, Amma's Diwali smell of cardamom and roasted gram flour.

qa.q: What did nineteen-year-old Deepak think and feel as he sat on the stairs?
qa.a: He thought six months of progress were gone and felt ashamed, as if the sudden tears meant he had gone backwards.

qa.q: What could have helped Deepak on those stairs that day?
qa.a: Knowing that grief comes in waves would have let him see the tears as a normal surge rather than a failure, and he could have told a friend what the smell had stirred.

qa.q: How might a classmate in that chemistry lecture have seen Deepak walking out?
qa.a: A classmate might have been confused or worried, seeing only sudden tears and not knowing that the smell of the laddoos had brought back Amma's death.

grounding: Shows a sudden wave of grief triggered by a festival smell in a lecture hall, and the false feeling of having gone backwards.

The client call was in ten minutes, and Hansa's slides still had a typo on page four. Then the pantry speaker, playing someone's old-songs list, started the harmonium opening of the ghazal her Papa used to hum while shaving.
Seven months, and she had not cried at work once. Now her eyes spilled over before she could stop them. She stood frozen at the whiteboard, marker in hand, thinking, I was doing so well. Why now?
Arohi, from the next desk, glanced over and quietly turned the speaker down. "Want me to open the call while you wash your face?"
Hansa nodded. In the washroom she pressed a wet tissue to her eyes and whispered, "Seven months," as though the number should have protected her.
Four minutes later she walked back in, fixed the typo and unmuted, still not sure what had just happened to her.

Rehana, you said the fourteenth is coming and you're dreading it. People at this branch think Jyoti ma'am never cries, so let me tell you what I did at twenty-one, the year after my younger brother Sunny died.
The first anniversary ambushed me. I went to college as usual and broke down in the library, and spent the whole evening angry at myself.
So the next year I planned it. I told my roommate Farida the date weeks in advance. We took the day off, cooked his favourite rajma-chawal, badly, and walked to the lake where he used to fly kites. When the tears came at the lake, I didn't scold myself. I said out loud, "This is grief, not weakness." Farida just held the umbrella.
And you know, it passed quicker than the library had. I still take that walk every March.
So. What would you want on your fourteenth?

qa.q: Where did Jyoti and Farida walk on the anniversary?
qa.a: To the lake where Sunny used to fly kites.

qa.q: Why did Jyoti say 'This is grief, not weakness' out loud at the lake?
qa.a: She wanted to stop scolding herself for crying, and naming the tears as grief let her feel them without shame.

qa.q: What step could Rehana take before the fourteenth, based on Jyoti's story?
qa.a: Rehana could pick a friend and a small ritual ahead of time, so the date is planned rather than an ambush.

The date sheet came out and Ritu's stomach dropped: the statistics exam fell on 9 November, one year since Ma. There was no changing it.
So she planned the day the way she planned revision. The night before, she lit a small diya beside Ma's photo and made poha, too salty, the way Ma always did. She messaged Zubin: "Tomorrow is the day. Chai after the exam?" He wrote back, "Already blocked it. I'll be at the gate."
Halfway through question three, her eyes blurred. Ritu put her pen down, let two tears fall onto the rough sheet, and whispered, "Grief. Okay." Then she breathed out and picked the pen up again.
At the gate, Zubin held out a paper cup without a word, and she found she could talk about Ma for a whole hour.

qa.q: Which exam fell on the anniversary of Ma's death?
qa.a: The statistics exam, on 9 November.

qa.q: What did Ritu's whisper 'Grief. Okay.' show about how she felt about crying in the exam hall?
qa.a: She accepted the tears as grief instead of judging them, which let the wave pass so she could keep writing.

qa.q: Which parts of Ritu's plan helped, and what could she add another year?
qa.a: Telling Zubin ahead and doing a small ritual the night before meant she wasn't ambushed; another year she could also let a teacher or counsellor know if an exam clashes with the date.

grounding: Illustrates expecting a hard date, planning it with a friend and a ritual, and letting tears come without judging them.

passage:
Dear Mridul,
It's been five weeks since Papa died, and I haven't told anyone this.
For two years I slept on the folding cot beside his bed at home. I woke for every cough and learned the beeps of his oxygen machine better than my own phone.
The morning after the funeral, I slept nine hours straight. I woke up and felt light. Relieved. And then I felt sick about feeling it.
What kind of son is glad his father is gone?
But I'm not glad he's gone. I miss his terrible jokes, the way he said, "Eshu, come, sit." I cry in the shower most days.
Both are true, and I've been hiding the relief like it's something dirty. Writing it to you is the first time it has felt a little lighter.
You sat with him on Sundays so I could rest. Maybe you understand.
Eshaan

qa.q: How long did Eshaan sleep the morning after the funeral?
qa.a: He slept nine hours straight.

qa.q: Why did Eshaan feel sick after feeling relieved?
qa.a: He felt ashamed, as if a good son shouldn't feel light after his father's death, even though he misses Papa and cries most days.

qa.q: What turning point does writing this letter open for Eshaan?
qa.a: Saying the relief to someone who knew Papa lets the shame lose some weight; talking more with Mridul, or later with a grief counsellor, can keep it from staying hidden.

qa.q: How might Mridul feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Mridul, who sat with Papa on Sundays, may feel trusted and moved, and may even recognise some of the same mixed feelings about the long illness ending.

grounding: Shows a caregiver feeling relief after a long illness ends, then shame about that relief, and the first step of not hiding it.

You want the honest version, Rafiq? Okay.
When Dadi died in March, after three years of forgetting my name, my Bua hugged me at the cremation and said, "Jahnavi, you were such a good granddaughter." And all I could think was, I get my evenings back. I can take the Bengaluru job.
Then I went home and couldn't eat. Because what kind of person thinks that at her Dadi's pyre?
I haven't said this to anyone. Not Papa. Not even my therapist.
I do miss her. I miss her humming while she oiled my hair, back when she still knew me. But I also miss sleeping. Both feel true, and I keep swallowing one of them.
...You're not looking at me like I'm a monster.
Huh. That actually helps.

qa.a: "Jahnavi, you were such a good granddaughter."

Every first Sunday, Nkechi makes her mum's jollof rice in the tiny flat kitchen in Leeds, and every first Sunday she lets the bottom burn a little, on purpose.
"That crispy layer was the best bit," she tells Hana, scraping it into two bowls.
Six years ago she couldn't walk past the rice aisle. In her second year, when she still couldn't sleep or make it to lectures, her GP pointed her to a bereavement counsellor, and those Thursday sessions are part of why she can stand at this stove now.
Today she laughs telling Hana how her mum sang loudly and badly while stirring. Her eyes sting halfway through the story, and she lets them.
Later she video-calls her brother in Lagos to argue about how much pepper is too much, then goes back to her thesis draft. Her mum would have wanted it finished.

At the community centre in Dehradun, the last child packed up her geometry box, and Sahil stayed back, wiping the whiteboard slowly.
Dolma, who runs the Saturday library next door, leaned in. "You always stay late. Why?"
"My father did," Sahil said. "He taught maths at a government school for thirty years and never left while a kid still had a doubt. He died when I was eighteen."
"Is it hard, doing his thing?"
"It was. For two years I couldn't even open his notebooks. The college counsellor helped me get unstuck." He smiled. "Now when a kid finally gets fractions, it's like he's in the room. It stings a bit and feels good at the same time."
Dolma nodded. "Six years is a long time to keep someone that close."
"He's in how I teach," Sahil said, capping the marker. "That's enough."

qa.q: What does Dolma run next door?
qa.a: The Saturday library.

qa.q: What does Sahil mean when he says it 'stings a bit and feels good at the same time'?
qa.a: He feels both the ache of missing his father and warmth that his father's way of teaching lives on through him.

qa.q: What helped Sahil when his grief was stuck, and what could someone in that place do?

Four months after Eshaan's sister Pooja died, the office had gone back to normal. People asked about the quarterly report, not about her.
Chinmay didn't. On Monday he stopped at Eshaan's desk with two steel boxes. "My mother made extra aloo paratha. Lunch on the terrace?"
Up there, he asked, "How are you today? Not in general. Today."
Eshaan shrugged. "Today's okay. Yesterday was bad. Her birthday's next week."
"Pooja would've made us all wear party hats," Chinmay said, and Eshaan laughed, surprised.
"Nobody says her name anymore. It's like she got deleted."
"Then I'll keep saying it. And Thursday, a walk after work? Same as last Thursday."
Eshaan nodded, tearing the paratha slowly. It wasn't a big thing. It was the fourth Thursday in a row.

Dear Elizabeth,
I know it's been seven months since your mum Margaret died, and I know most people have stopped asking. I haven't stopped thinking about her. Yesterday I passed the bakery where she always bought those awful coconut buns, and I laughed out loud remembering her defending them.
I'm not writing to ask how you are "in general". I'm asking how today is. Just today. You can answer in one word.
I'm making biryani on Saturday, far too much as usual. Can I bring a box over? Or would you rather come for a walk by the canal on Sunday morning? Or both. Or neither, and I'll ask again in two weeks.
No need to reply quickly.
With love,
Salma

qa.a: By the canal on Sunday morning.

qa.q: Why does Salma tell Elizabeth about the coconut buns?
qa.a: Salma wants Elizabeth to know Margaret is still remembered and talked about, even though most people have stopped asking. 🤍

Class 11 observation note, Disha Menon, class teacher, 14 August
Mehak has had three colds since June. Today she arrived with a flask of strong coffee, her second before first period, she told me. She used to stay back for sitar practice every Wednesday but has skipped it for five weeks. "I don't enjoy it anymore, and there's no time anyway," she said.
In maths she put her head down twice. When I asked about sleep she laughed. "Four hours. It's fine, ma'am. I've just been lazy this term, so I'm studying till two to catch up."
She seemed to truly believe the tiredness was her own fault.
What I did next: I told her that tiredness is a signal, not laziness, and asked her to meet the school counsellor with me on Friday. She agreed, a little reluctantly. I will also call her mother this evening to share what I have seen and ask how things look at home.

qa.q: How many hours of sleep did Mehak say she was getting?
qa.a: Four hours.

qa.q: Why does Mehak keep studying till two despite being so tired?
qa.a: She believes her tiredness means she has been lazy, so she thinks the answer is to push harder.

qa.q: What did Disha Menon do at this stage, and why does it fit?
qa.a: She told Mehak tiredness is a signal, set up a counsellor meeting and planned to call her mother, catching the pattern before it deepens.

qa.q: What might Mehak's mother experience when the teacher calls?
qa.a: She may be surprised or worried to hear about the colds, the coffee and the dropped sitar, and may start to see the late nights at home differently.

grounding: Shows a student running on coffee and late nights, catching repeated colds, losing joy in a hobby and reading exhaustion as laziness.

At the block office in Kuttanad, the ceiling fan turned slowly over stacks of crop-loss forms. Anjali had been interning there for four months, and she no longer read the farmers' names before stamping.
Joseph, the other intern, came in with mud to his ankles. "Chechi from the east paddy says the new drainage is working! She wants us to come and see."
Anjali didn't look up. "Great. Another photo for a report nobody in the head office opens."
"You used to love the field visits."
"I used to think they mattered." She stamped another form.
Joseph stood there a moment, his excitement draining, then went back out.
At the tea shop later she laughed with the clerk about "Saint Joseph and his drains". Walking home along the canal, she felt nothing about any of it, and the nothing felt safer than caring.

passage:
Wednesday night
Today a two-line email took me forty minutes. I rewrote it six times and still sent it with Swati ma'am's name spelled wrong.
Then I mixed up the March and April sheets in the reconciliation. She caught it before the client did, thank god, but she looked at me like she was trying to work out what had happened to me.
What happened is I'm a fraud. Three months ago I was the intern who finished early. Now I can't add a column without checking it three times, and I still get it wrong.
So I stayed till 9 redoing everything, then came home and couldn't even remember what I'd redone.
The harder I try, the worse it gets. Maybe I'm just not good at this.
Swati ma'am said, "Let's talk tomorrow, 10 am." I'm dreading it.
Neelam

qa.q: How long did the two-line email take?
qa.a: The two-line email took forty minutes.

qa.q: What does Neelam believe is behind the mistakes?
qa.a: Neelam believes being a fraud and 'not good at this' is the reason, without seeing that exhaustion is making everything slower.

qa.q: What might a helpful 10 am talk with Swati ma'am look like?
qa.a: Neelam could admit how tired everything feels, and Swati ma'am could look at the workload and rest together with Neelam rather than asking for more effort.

qa.q: How might Swati ma'am see the change in Neelam?
qa.a: She has watched an intern who once finished early start making repeated mistakes, so she may be puzzled and concerned rather than angry, which is why she asked to talk.

grounding: Shows simple tasks taking far longer, errors multiplying and a sense of being a fraud, with longer hours only deepening the exhaustion.

Jahnavi: rafiq are you still in the lab
Rafiq: leaving in 10. why
Jahnavi: I messed up the titration AGAIN. third time
Jahnavi: it's the same experiment I did in first year with my eyes closed
Rafiq: hey, it happens
Jahnavi: it doesn't happen to me. or it didn't. my lab report took all sunday and I still got the units wrong
Jahnavi: I feel like everyone's going to figure out I got in by luck
Rafiq: you topped the batch in 2nd year, jahnavi
Jahnavi: exactly. and now look. I just need to put in more hours
Rafiq: you've been putting in more hours for a month. has it helped?
Jahnavi: ...no
Rafiq: then maybe hours aren't the fix. come get chai. tomorrow we talk to Dr Kulkarni about the workload
Jahnavi: ok 😔
Rafiq: 🙂 5 min, main gate

qa.q: What is Jahnavi afraid everyone will figure out?
